utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record all the accused are here. Minus Beara. Accused Beara. What's the problem with your client, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a very good question. One of the guards said he was sick. He didn't call me, and I understand that there has been no waiver faxed. So I'd asked Yaiza earlier to see if -- call the UNDU to see if they've had a waiver faxed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are told that a waiver will be arriving in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'd like to see a copy of it when it comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic. That's about it. The Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer and no one else. You know that we have a technical problem this morning. And we have waited for one hour to see if it could be fixed. We are told that no solution has been found so far. The effect or the consequences of this technical hitch that we have encountered are the following: That although the proceedings are being transcribed, are being recorded, in other words, although a transcript does exist and will continue to exist throughout the sitting, none of us, that includes ourselves, will be able to see the transcript visually on our screens, both screens. We have thought about the possibility, various options that we have, and we have been also told that there is some reluctance on the part of some of the Defence teams to proceed without a transcript. I would like to know precisely what the objection is so that we'll be able to decide what weight to give it and then take a decision on whether to proceed with the sitting or not. We have also been told that from the Prosecution side there is no position to the sitting proceeding with the testimony of General Smith. From the Defence teams, is there anyone who doesn't wish the proceedings to go ahead? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I cannot follow the transcript and I cannot remember exact phrases and exact translations after the whole testimony of the witness and compare it with the transcript when I got it, when I get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should that worry you today? You're not going to cross-examine this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this witness has to return and the transcript will be available this afternoon or at latest tomorrow in any case. You are not going to cross-examine the witness tomorrow. You are not going to cross-examine the witness the day after. It will be quite sometime before you cross-examine this witness, by which time would you have had ample opportunity to go through the transcript, and you will be receiving audio interpretation of his testimony as you go along. And you're not going to receive at any time a transcript in B/C/S of what he is saying. Because the transcript will be in English in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I'll get this transcript later this day. All right. I'll not object in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Does anybody else object? The understanding is of course the transcript will be available in any case. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, we don't object, Your Honour, but could I invite my learned friend Mr. Thayer to go particularly slowly because I for one am going to need to make some sort of long hand note in the way that I have done over the last 20 years in practice prior to coming here frankly, and I've got no problem with that but one does need to go a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's fair enough. Mr. Thayer, you agree to that? All right. Anyone else wishes to raise an objection? Thank you. And to put the accused's mind at rest, you will be able to follow the proceedings because you will be receiving interpretation in any case. So next thing now before we start with General Smith, we will need to reorganise a little bit the schedule for today. Let's start first and in the course of the sitting, we'll communicate to you how we intend to sit but the idea is to -- now that we have lost one hour to try and recuperate as much as we can. I take it there are no further -- no preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: None. Okay. So Madam Usher, if you could bring in General Smith, please? Mr. Popovic. Why are you not hearing -- why don't you have your headphones where they should be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they are not comfortable when they are on my head, but I can hear quite well with the headphones as they are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. I wish to apologise to you first and foremost for the delay. We had a technical hitch. We still have it, but we have discussed it with the parties and now there is agreement that we can proceed notwithstanding the continuation of the technical problem that we have. Only problem that exists also for you is that while usually you would be able to follow the proceedings on the two screens that you have in front of you, today, a transcript will not be rolling at all and therefore you won't be able to follow the proceeding except apart from what you would be hearing. Before you start giving evidence, you're required to make a solemn declaration, the text of which is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. What's going to happen is that you're going to start your testimony today then the understanding is that you will return later on to continue it and to be cross-examined also at a later stage. Mr. Thayer will go first. Since we don't have a transcript facilities today, and we would need to take notes in longhand, I suggest that in your answers, you try to slow down a little bit so that no one will have big problems. And you also speak the same language, both Mr. Thayer and yourself, and therefore always allow a short pause between question and answer because the interpreters need that. Otherwise we'll have problems. For the rest, we will sit now until 11.40, and we'll have a 30 minute break after that and then we'll sit from 12.10 to quarter to 2.00. All right? And that way we would recuperate, recover a little bit of the lost time. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning again to you and Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My name is Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, we've lost a little bit of time, so I'm going to I think move a little more quickly through your educational and background and military service history. I'll try to summarise that quickly but if I've gotten anything wrong, please feel free to correct me. Sir, you were born in 1943, graduated Haileybury and the Imperial Service college and then Sandhurst. You enlisted in the British army in 1962 and were commissioned into the parachute regiment in 1964. Your service has brought you to Africa, the Middle East, Europe, the Caribbean, and Asia. Specifically, looking at the last ten years of your service, you were General officer commanding the first armoured division from 1990 to 1992, including the Gulf War. You served as assistant chief of Defence Staff for operations from 1992 to 1994, and we'll get back to that in a moment. You commanded UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina during the year of 1995. You were general officer commanding in Northern Ireland from 1996 to 1998. And you served as deputy supreme commander allied powers Europe from 1998 to 2001, covering NATO's Balkan operations. And you retired at the rank of Lieutenant General in January of 2002. Is that a correct summary, General, of your service? Anything you would care to add?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Two corrections. I retired as a general, not a Lieutenant General. And the full title of the appointment in the Ministry of Defence in 1992 was the assistant chief of the Defence Staff for operations and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, what kind of work do you do now?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'm a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to your time with the Ministry of Defence, just prior to your service in Sarajevo. When you were at MOD, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you did?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps the easiest way of describing my job, which was a new job, a new appointment in the ministry, it had been created as a result of the experience of the 1991 Gulf War - and I had never worked in the Ministry of Defence before - and the job was essentially to be the operations officer for all of the United Kingdom armed forces; and thus every operation we were conducting to a greater or lesser extent was -- went over my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what involvement if any did you have in operations pertaining to the former Yugoslavia, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: In the sense that these operations were -- the British side of these operations, I was involved in the policy, the deployment of forces and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you give the Trial Chamber, please, an idea of some specific examples of topics or areas in which you were involved specifically having to do with the former Yugoslavia when you were chief of operations for the staff?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There was the initial deployment -- we already had a -- I should start with, we already had a deployment in Croatia when I was starting this job, this appointment. There was the deployment -- the initial deployment of a battle group to Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of UNPROFOR. There was the -- and the associated work with that. There was all the negotiations and staff work involved with, including NATO in the operations, such as the no-fly zones, the safe areas, exclusion zones, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there also involvement to some degree with the so-called contact group, the Trial Chamber may be hearing references here or there to it, and if there was such involvement, can you explain what it was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved with the contact group but in support -- this was -- the dealing with the contact group was conducted by another department, the foreign office, and I would be there as the military adviser in support of the foreign office official who would be doing the actual dealings with the contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the contact group, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The contact group was formed by a number of nations after the United States had refused to accept the Vance-Owen Plan in, if my memory is correct, 1993. The countries in the initial grouping of countries in the group was, from memory, the United States, Russia, Britain, France and Germany, and the idea of the contact group was to stay in contact with each other, hence its name, those countries to stay in contact with each other and to coordinate their policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the date you took command of UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It's late January 1995 and I think it's the 26th but it might -- I might be wrong by a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where were you headquartered, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The -- my headquarters was in Sarajevo itself, in the residency. There was a rare headquarters down in Split but my particular bit of it was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was your predecessor?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My predecessor was a general, Sir Michael Rose. He at the time was a lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Sarajevo, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My immediate superior was General Janvier in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there a UN civilian leadership above you as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There was the Secretary-General's special representative, Mr. Akashi in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom did Mr. Akashi report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: He reported to the Secretary-General back in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, when it came to decisions of magnitude, where were those decisions taken, in Sarajevo where were you based, or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by magnitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let my give you an example. For example, if close air support were called for somewhere within your area of command, where would that decision be taken ultimately?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to differentiate between close air support and other forms of aerial attack. If it was close air support in direct defence of UNPROFOR forces, then that could be called for by anybody. There were decisions to be made by -- as to whether or not it was -- the call would be answered up the chain of command, and strictly, that never changed. What happened was that over the year of 1995 until after the London Conference in July, this decision became increasingly held by the political chain of command, but the other forms of aerial attack they are still dropping bombs but their purpose of them such as enforcing the exclusion zone would be an example. This was always a higher-level decision than just calling for close air support, and after May, end of May 1995, that decision had to all intents and purposes been moved to Boutros-Ghali, the Secretary-General in New York, and remained there until after the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we may recur to some of those topics later. When you arrived in Sarajevo, General, did you have a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have more than one during the year of your service?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. They changed every six months, and I had three.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall their names and the -- I'm sorry, General, we have an interruption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Yes, General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but could we stick to what we had agreed; that Mr. Thayer should slow down a little and the General Rupert Smith as well so we can note things down? This is no different from any other examination. I think it is going even a little faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, and I had the same feeling too. You had forgotten all about what I had stated earlier, so please do slow down both of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you recall the names of your chiefs of staff and approximately when they served?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The only one I can immediately remember is the middle one, General Nicolai, and he served in -- as my Chief of Staff from approximately March until September of that year, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you also have a military assistant during your service?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I had a military assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Again, I had two of them, one after the other. The first was Colonel Baxter and the second Colonel Carleton [phoen]. My memory is that Baxter left either at end of September early October and Carleton came after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina being based in Sarajevo, was there a subordinate sector based in Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Sector Sarajevo had its own headquarters, and that too was in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you co-located or was sector Sarajevo in a separate location?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It was in a separate location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that location?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think, if my memory is correct, in the PTT building. It was certainly down in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall who commanded sector Sarajevo during the period of your service, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There were three commanders during my time there. The first was Brigadier General Gobillard, the second Brigadier General Bashley [phoen], and I can't remember the third one, but he came in I think November.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you took command of UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina, what generally speaking, was the military-political situation you were facing in January, February of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The general situation was that there had been signed recently a Cessation of Hostilities Agreement between the federation and the Bosnian Serbs. The -- and by and large that was holding when I took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in connection with that Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, General, was there a process of meetings that had been designed to implement that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that process have a name and can you describe for the Trial Chamber whether that process was working during your time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It did have a name. It was something like the joint commission but I can't remember the full title. And it failed -- the process, as it was intended, failed to work. It didn't function during -- it wasn't functioning when I took over, and it didn't get any better in the subsequent weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the idea behind this joint commission?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Again, I'd need to look at the old -- the agreement to be precise about this, but the general idea was that at this commission the two sides would sort out those issues that were still -- that might occur as to why fighting should start again, and they would sort them out within that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, soon after your arrival, did you begin meeting with various civilian and military leaders of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There was a programme that I went through of meeting principal actors in -- on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please just name some of the individuals on both sides, both from the civilian and military leadership, of the Bosnian Muslim side and the Bosnian Serb side with whom you met?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Taking them in the order you've mentioned, the president Izetbegovic. Muratovic was the minister with particular responsibility for dealing with the UN. Silajdzic. General Delic would be four that come to mind on, if you like, the Sarajevo side. In Pale, I met Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, Mladic, for four names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were these meetings sometimes also attended by civilian UN officials?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: In almost all cases, if I had a civil affairs, political affairs, UN officials in my headquarters, I would take them with me and in those early days, I certainly had UN officials with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall just some of the names of those people who accompanied you from time to time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The principal one in those early days was Enrique Aguilar, a Mexican. A bit later on Diane Mehoff [phoen] who came from Bulgaria, if I recall correctly. Then there's a gap. Antonio Pedwey [phoen] came subsequently. He would be there from about September. Those would be three names.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would Mr. Akashi be present sometimes for these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. He came to meetings but they were his meetings, though. He wasn't there in support of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And generally speaking, what was the reasons -- or what were the reasons for these meetings, particularly during the early period of your service in February and March and going into April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I understand my purpose in the meetings as opposed to the purpose of the joint commission or whatever these were called. This was my purpose. I was interested in meeting all these people and gaining an understanding of their position and what their intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This might be an obvious question, General, but why were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I had my own mission given to me, which was, in short, to see that humanitarian aid was delivered, to carry out the instructions of the Security Council in relation to the exclusion zones and safe areas, and to do that amidst a war, even if it had been a cease-fire in existence, I needed to understand the intentions and positions of the various parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was your effort at understanding the intentions of the various parties something that you tried to give form to or was it something that just took you from meeting to meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. I gave -- there was -- I had a fairly systematic approach to this effort, and so it had a form. I called it a thesis or my thesis, and it was used by me as a means of asking questions and looking for information so as to be able to clarify my thinking as to what was happening during those early weeks, and to project that into the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, would you describe your thesis and how it developed and the process by which you worked through your thesis over time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I will start with the process. Essentially, there was the daily reports. There was sources of information. There were my own officers and the sectors on the ground, with their headquarters all providing me with information as to what they thought was going on and what the people they dealt with were saying was going on. And then there were these contacts I was having with the leadership. And the -- the idea of the thesis, if I could just explain the theory, if you like, it had become my practice much earlier in my service that if I was faced with a situation that was not very clear to me, then I would establish a hypothesis, the most likely set of circumstances, and then collect information to either prove it right or wrong, and then keep adjusting it until I had a synthesis or the thesis that I would operate on. And this focused the work of my staff and of my own thinking. The -- in this particular case, it started to become clear to me, from these -- largely from these conversations with the leaderships, that no side to this conflict actually wanted to make peace at this stage, and that this Cessation of Hostilities Agreement would break down. And the evidence of it breaking down became more frequently available during February and March and early April. At its simplest, the Federation were beginning to gain strength and had been forced back into a small-enough area that their numerical superiority and the arms they were now getting were going to give them an advantage if they started to fight again, and they would be seeking, I thought, a -- to alter the situation to their advantage by armed force. On the other side, the Bosnian Serbs had got so much territory and had so few people that they were overextended, and they would have liked to have a cessation of hostilities to work so that that became the basis from which they could bargain from, but they weren't going to be allowed to do that. And the only way they could hold the territory that they had was that they needed to produce more soldiers, and that the running sore in their situation were the enclaves, specifically the enclaves in the east, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, which, from their point of view, lay in their year and required the -- a large number of forces and resources to guard. I therefore -- in the light of this, I came to the conclusion - and I assert, re-emphasise, that this was a thesis, I was quite prepared to discover other information to change my mind or my thinking about this, I didn't but that didn't stop me looking for it - that the -- not only was the probability that this cease-fire would break down, but in order to be able to hold the territory they had gained, that the Bosnian Serbs would, in the words I used at the time, squeeze the eastern enclaves, and that in order to reduce their significance and to bring -- and to free up forces so as to be able to defend the territory that had been gained or held from the Bosnian Muslims and the Federation generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, you referred to various sources of information that was coming to you or that you sought out during this process. Was that information both of a purely military nature, shall we say, or did it also include information of a larger political nature, if we can make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: We were certainly getting reporting from the UN chain of command, the civil side of the UN chain of command, there was a certain amount of national support available to the headquarters, British in my case, but the French would be getting French and so forth and so that got pooled, as much as it was able to be pooled, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how important, or not, was it to you to have an awareness of the political context in which these military developments were occurring?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It was very important to have that understanding. The position I was in was absolutely on the interface between the politics and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, what I'd like to do now is discuss with you some specific meetings that you had, beginning in March of 1995. And I want to turn your attention first to the first week of March and to a meeting you had with General Mladic in Jahorina. I want to ask you what if anything you recall about that particular meeting in Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The first thing I'd say of it was it was an important meeting in that it was one of those ones where I gained an understanding that helped to crystallise what I was talking about earlier, the thesis. From my memory, we realised this -- a meeting was taking place in Jahorina about -- during the period 24, 36 hours before I went to the one with Mladic. At the time, I had an officer on my staff whose -- called Mike Stanley, and he got up to Jahorina the night before I met with Mladic. We had also seen a number of vehicles with Belgrade plates and Russian vehicles from the Russian Battalion under my command, up at Jahorina in that period before. So we knew there was a big meeting going on with -- of some significance. My memory is that I was invited to come to Jahorina the next day. Whether the invite came the next -- that next day or the day before, I can't recall. When I got up there, I met with, first, Koljevic, and then Mladic and Koljevic together. And they wanted to tell me that a big decision had been made and that essentially they reckoned that the Federation would be going back to war and that the -- and that, secondly, the UN were part of the problem, if you like, that we were supplying the enclaves, we were causing-- we were keeping these groups of people alive from which operations were being conducted and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's actually take a look at some notes of that meeting. If we could have 65 ter number 2933 on e-court, please? General you should have a document showing up momentarily, and if it's easier to have a hard copy, I do have them available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't afford to lose or waste more time. If we have a hard copy, let's put it on the ELMO, please. This is going to come up. I am not receiving anything in any case. It is in the e-court. But put it on the ELMO and let's proceed that way for the time being. So, please try to locate it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check whether e-court is working or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see a reason why it shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's proceed in this manner. E-court, I'd like to see the B/C/S version so that the accused can follow, and we put the original English version on the ELMO. So English version on the ELMO. The ELMO is not working with the screen either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have the B/C/S version on e-court, please? It is working as well now. What we need is the B/C/S version. All right. E-court is working, as far as documents are concerned so we have the English version there. So if you have -- if you have the B/C/S version, you can put that on the ELMO instead. All right. Okay. B/C/S is available there as well. All right. Your next question? And sorry for this interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It is a report by my MA, Colonel Baxter, and we had the practice that he -- at the end of a meeting such as this, he would write a minute and it would be distributed to those who needed to know what had been said and done at the meeting, and this is one of those meetings -- such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber what the purpose of this account of the meeting was, for you, in terms of what you intended the document to do?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The purpose of this was that other people would know, other people in my command, and those who commanded me, would know what I had been doing, what I'd said, what -- and others had said at this meeting, so there was a record from which my own people could then act.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was of particular importance to you, if anything, about the way these reports were written?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the first thing is they should be a factual account but they should -- and record the essential points discussed, any decisions made and so on. But secondly, they should provide something of the atmosphere of the meeting, both in its overall setting, as well as in the actual atmospherics of the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you consider Colonel Baxter's skill in achieving that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I was content, happy, with his way he did it, and it is within my own army one of the functions of a military assistant, to do this and to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at this document, specifically at paragraph 1. It refers to the meeting between yourself and General Mladic. Now, other than his bodyguards, would General Mladic typically attend these meetings alone or would he be accompanied by any other VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. He was -- he would not hold these meetings on his own, and he -- I can't think of an occasion when he wasn't accompanied by another senior officer and it was frequently General Tolimir that is mentioned in this -- in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I note first that there is a reference in this paragraph 1, which is on page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S, to a conversation that you had with Mladic the day before, in which he approved a convoy for DutchBat resupply. General, do you recall anything in particular about that conversation you had with General Mladic the day before?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There were -- it was not only a convoy. It was for me to go as well, into Srebrenica. I had been trying to gain permission from Mladic almost since the very first days I was in command, to visit the eastern enclaves and the UNPROFOR forces in them that I commanded, and this -- in addition, and in particular in the case of the Srebrenica, they were very low on supplies. I can't remember the detail and exactly how low, but it was beginning to be something that was reported to me. And so on this occasion, as I recall it, both the need to get a convoy in and my wish to visit myself was a subject of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, without going into any specifics, because we'll do that in a moment, to what extent, if any, did the resupply of DutchBat's materiel and fuel become a topic of future meetings that you had with the Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, it continued to be a demand that we could get resupplies into our own forces in the enclaves quite apart from the demand to get the humanitarian convoys in, which were also being denied. And in this particular case, there was a humanitarian element to the request, as I recall it again. Medecins Sans Frontieres were short of medical supplies, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may, let's turn to page 2 of this document, and that's page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, and look at paragraph 4. Okay. I see we have both versions up now. General, the first line of paragraph 4 indicates that the bulk of the meeting and evidently the main issue Mladic wished to discuss was the effect of sanctions on the Bosnian Serbs. What are the sanctions that are being referred to here? And why were they in place? Just briefly, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There were a series of sanction measures, and they go back to the very beginning of the -- of this crisis. There was -- that had been placed not only the Bosnian Serbs but on Serbia. As to the movement of weapons and so on and so forth. I'd have to go back and read the documents to be more detailed and precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, towards the end of that paragraph, it indicates that General Mladic then threatened a blockade of all enclaves, including Sarajevo, if sanctions were not lifted. And if we look at the bottom of page 2 of the English, it indicates that he demanded acceptance of his terms by 15 March, after which he would impose a blockade on all enclaves. And we have to go to the next page of the B/C/S to pick that up, and end of the English. Now, General, what was your response to General Mladic's threat of a blockade?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I pointed out that he would be in effect attacking the international community by doing this, and there would be at some point there is consequences of that. Secondly, he was preventing me from doing what I'd been told to do. And that the next stage, if I can't do this, would be to start to use air resupply and if that was attacked, he would involve NATO because NATO would then become -- would be flying in support of the helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we turn to paragraph 7, and that's at page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S, that's just at the bottom of the page, there is a reference to another meeting being scheduled for the 7th of March, which was to follow your visit to Srebrenica on the 6th and 7th. You've already alluded to the permission that General Mladic had granted to you to visit Srebrenica. Did you in fact visit the enclave, sir, on those dates?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And there was at least one, if not two, supply vehicles came with me into the enclave. They came on different routes, if I recall correctly, and I did visit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you visit both the town itself of Srebrenica as well as the DutchBat base?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I was visiting primarily the unit, but in doing so, I was shown the town, I met various officials, inspected the weapon collection point and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you first describe for the Trial Chamber your recollections of the DutchBat base and the situation that you observed there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The entry into the enclave was through a specific check-point which was -- clearly controlled all movement by UNPROFOR and supply convoys in and out of the enclave. And I can't remember whether it was on my way out or my way in, but one of the vehicles with me, one of the supply vehicles, had a very detailed search and inspection carried out on it by that check-point. The Dutch Battalion was stationed at a place called Potocari which was outside the town of Srebrenica itself in an old factory. There was a number of portocabin type structures around the old factory as well but that's where they were stationed. In the town itself -- the town itself was largely built up in -- along one long road running up this valley with the houses all around it. And then around the outside of the enclave, but particularly on the side nearest the town, there were a -- a series of OPs of which I went and visited, I think, two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Just wanted to inform you that for a short while we did get something like 20 lines of transcript but it was only for a short time and it stuck again so that if you can identify what happened during that short interval, maybe you found a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see a reference to Ms. Baxendale on my transcript, so I'm not sure what we're getting but hope springs eternal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Nothing to do with this case, okay. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, would you describe the state of affairs as you found them among the DutchBat contingent that you visited in terms of their supplies and operational capacity?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: When the battalion had deployed, and my memory is that they replaced a Canadian unit, the Bosnian Serbs had prevented all their initial supplies and some of their ammunition and weapons from being deployed into the enclave. So there was a basic shortage of certain items already. They had not been supplied with a number of things, and particular concern was fuel, for some time and again I can't remember the precise details. And there was a limited supply of certain natures of ammunition as a result of the initial failure to get the kit into the enclave in the first place. They weren't starving, but there certainly wasn't much variation in the diet or anything like that at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to bringing in some medical supplies for Medecins Sans Frontieres. Did you visit with any NGOs while you were in Srebrenica, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember visiting specific NGOs. I remember representatives of the NGOs all coming together at the battalion headquarters at some stage when I was there and meeting them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did they describe -- I'm sorry, I'll try to leave more of a pause. Did they describe what their situation was, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd also knew this to some extent from the reporting in my own headquarters. Both UNHCR who was responsible for getting food in had been reporting a shortage of the basic rations being got into the enclave, and there was this shortfall in certain medical supplies and again I cannot remember the precise details of that, and -- but my memory is that one of those trucks that we brought was -- contained medical supplies for Medecins Sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've already noted that a meeting was scheduled for the 7th of March. Did you, in fact, meet with General Mladic again on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we met at Vlasenica as planned, on my way out of-- from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not you conveyed your impressions of Srebrenica to General Mladic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall it precisely as you stated it, but we undoubtedly discussed the situation of the enclaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what if anything he said to you with respect to resupplying the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: My memory of that meeting was it was more of the -- of the line of the Jahorina meeting, that these enclaves are a great nuisance in my rear. This is Mladic talking. And "I am going to prevent them from being a problem to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another report. This is 65 ter number 2934, if we may have that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The number is 2934.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I note that this refers to the meeting on 7 March between yourself and General Mladic. Let's just move along, General, if we could, to the bottom of page 1, which is paragraph 4, and that's page 2 of the B/C/S. It notes that you asked or General Mladic asked you for his -- for your impressions of your visit, and you registered your concern over the shortages of the medical supplies and general supply shortages. If we turn to page 2 of the English, and I think we can stay with the B/C/S, the report notes that at this stage, Mladic reported that he had cleared food and medicine convoys to Srebrenica and Zepa over the last 24 hours. What if anything, General, did this tell you, given your prior conversation on the 4th of March, in which General Mladic had cleared a convoy? What if anything did this tell you about his ability or authority to approve or restrict the resupply of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it confirmed a long-standing view held by my predecessor, quite apart from myself, that Mladic was very much in charge and that these restrictions and orders were centrally controlled and controlled by him and his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this meeting, General, do you recall General Mladic telling you anything about his intentions regarding the size or the boundaries of the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. At the risk of talking about ground without a map, between the enclave of Srebrenica and to its south the enclave of Zepa, was an east-west road, that was important to the Serbs. The road was outside the boundaries of the enclave of Srebrenica, but could be overlooked by the Bosniak positions in the enclave. It could be overlooked and attacked. And this was a cause of concern to Mladic, and I must assume his subordinate commanders in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at paragraph 5 here of the English page 2 and same page for the B/C/S, thank you. There is a reference to an UNPROFOR OP or OPs in the area of this road that you described. And then there is a reference to a presentation by General Mladic. Can you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber what that presentation entailed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The essential point of his argument was that -- was twofold. The first was that the UN had allowed the Bosnian defenders of Srebrenica in this particular case to expand the area of the safe area to their advantage, to wit, in this case, overlooking this particular road. And the second point was that the safe areas in his view were a great deal smaller than they were now, and he indicated on the map just how small in his view they really were. And I think in this paragraph we -- Baxter put them in. Yes, he does, about in the middle, the safe areas comprise a limited area, Srebrenica 4 and a half kilometres by one kilometre and so forth. Those were being -- those were indicated to us at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look further down in this report, it indicates that Mladic explained that he would attack into the enclaves to destroy the Armija, but would respect his interpretation of the boundaries of the safe areas. What did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you must remember that although I took of the thesis now as though it was a formed idea, it wasn't anything of the sort. This was an idea that's in the process of constant development. The meeting in Jahorina, my drives through Bosnian Serb territory to Srebrenica, the -- and this particular meeting, were all giving me more information against which to test the thesis. And here was a -- here was the commander, Mladic, telling me what I had already started to form an idea as to what he would be doing, which was to squeeze the safe areas, to squeeze the enclaves, to make them less of a problem in his rear area. And so this -- I was assessing what he was saying in that light.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, General, you just referred to your drives through Bosnian Serb-held territory. What if anything about those drives added or subtracted as it might have been, from your thesis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It was its emptiness. There was -- there were very, very few people about and the people you saw were not males of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did tell you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: That there was a shortage of manpower to defend the area that they had taken, and they needed to find a way of freeing up forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The report goes on to state that these concerns had led him, General Mladic, to restrict the amount of food, medicine, and fuel destined for the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall him telling you that, and if so, what was your response, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I explained that, you know, you -- this again would be a question -- would be interpreted as an attack on the safe areas by the international community, by the Security Council and so forth, and that in the long term this was not in the interests of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you a couple of questions about this later but with respect to this observation post along this east-west communication, do you recall what eventually happened to that OP in the south of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. It got attacked, and if my memory is correct, shot up by a Bosnian Serb tank, and the occupants subsequently withdrew. I'm not sure when that occurred, but it's before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally on this document, General, there is a comment at the end of paragraph 5. It deals with your interpretation of this exchange with General Mladic. Is there anything you care to add or elaborate upon to this interpretation that may have betrayed's General Mladic's capacity or lack thereof to fight a two-front war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: What you see here is the thesis being formed. I'm talking after the event. This is a report being written in the event. And here you can see my military assistant in effect saying what I've just been saying, that we were beginning to put together that what's being said to us and so forth as to support the idea that the -- there wasn't enough forces for the Bosnian Serbs to do what they were going to need to do if they didn't squeeze the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that in addition to the high military command of the Bosnian Serbs, you also met with their political leadership. I want to turn your attention to a meeting you had with President Karadzic at a hotel near Pale on the 5th of April. This was a meeting where you were accompanied by one person each. Do you recall this meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Specifically, no. I remember there was a series of these meetings during April and I think early May, and they would have started in early April. So I imagine the one you're referring to is the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll then look at some of these individual meeting reports. Was there a reason that you met under these circumstances with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: (A), I wanted to go on talking to the Bosnian Serbs. It was part of my understanding the situation. But also to try and play my part in support of Mr. Akashi and others in furthering the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. And so I was interested in having these conversations with everybody, quite apart from the military commanders. The -- my memory is that it was the President Karadzic himself who wanted to meet in this way and in that hotel. He was the one, I think, who dictated the venue and the attendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look, General, at 65 ter number 2935. Okay. I see we have the B/C/S up now as well. Do you see the report before you, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It notes that this is a summary of the meeting or starts with a summary of the meeting between yourself and President Karadzic, and it indicates that it was secret and private. Now, again, was that secrecy and privacy your choice or President Karadzic's choice?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think it was his, his choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have any insight at the time as to why he wanted to meet in secret?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think my recall of this, I think he was -- he found it easier to deal in a small group than with everybody around him, and I think at the time we thought that there was a certain amount of tension between the political and military in Pale as to how to deal with this crisis that they were approaching, that they'd were either - and I think by now the Bosnians have actually attacked or they knew an attack was imminent - I can't remember the chronology very precisely. But either towards the end of March or very early April the Bosnians have actually carried out an attack and I think this is after that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the actual document. It indicates that President Karadzic was accompanied by Dr. Zametica. I want to direct your attention to paragraph 3 of the English, and if we could scroll up on the B/C/S, perfect, thank you. It indicates that you expressed serious concerns regarding recent activities of the VRS, specifically an increasing number of attacks on safe areas, direct targeting of UNPROFOR personnel and disruption of humanitarian aid convoys. And it indicates that you explained that eventually you would be forced to respond by NATO air strikes. Do you recall what President Karadzic told you about the supplies in the enclaves, his view of the resupply situation in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think this is not only his, it was -- I think there was a general view that we were in effect supplying the Bosnian defenders, we, the UN, that was, and that we were taking in, as it were, extra staff to supply them so that the defence of the safe area would be -- would be supported. I don't remember the particular points in this meeting, but I dare say the documents will show us that he had the view.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at the top of page 2 of the English, he specifies that he would not facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid while the Bosnian Serbs were under blockade. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes. But that was -- yes. But that was part of the arguments of Jahorina as well, that generally, that if this is being done to us, we're not going to help anyone else either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, that was a separate issue from the resupply of the UNPROFOR forces, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down to paragraph 9 just for a moment, and that's going to be running from pages 2 to 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One problem. No, no I thought I heard General Miletic. You're okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We cannot follow, neither I nor the others, if they are not switching pages, and he doesn't really care whether we follow or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go ahead. I think you can follow now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are looking at paragraph 9, the bottom of page 1 of the English, and we are set with the B/C/S. The first line of paragraph 9 indicates that President Karadzic was at pains to point out the decision had been made to start a counteroffensive. And if we move to the last page of the English and if we move to the next page of the B/C/S at paragraph 10, there is a notation that President Karadzic expressed no concern about the threat of NATO and announced a clear preparedness to take NATO on. General, given these expressions by President Karadzic, what conclusion or inference did you draw from this encounter as to where things stood with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I see from this that that attack had occurred so, the one I meant -- the Bosnians had started an offensive. Well, to all intents and purposes, the cease-fire had now broken down. It takes the rest of this month of April for everyone to recognise it but that's -- this is the beginning of the end. Certainly, the -- and here I found it difficult to remember what I thought in April 1995, when I now know what happened later that year, let alone what I've heard since, but my -- I think my understanding at the time was that here was more of what we were already starting to see in late February and March, and certainly since that Jahorina meeting and my trip into Srebrenica, that the Bosnian Serbs were going to counterattack, were going to put the pressure on to the safe areas, specifically those in the east, and that for them the UN and NATO were neutralised, they could control us, by means of restricting our freedom of movement and of restricting the supplies and so forth that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I note -- I think we are coming up on the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you've got about two, three minutes left before the break, but if you wish to stop here, we can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That would be preferable, Mr. President. We have another document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have strictly 30 minutes' break in order to try again to recover some of the lost time. Thank you. ---Recess taken at 11.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before we proceed, I'm pleased to announce that the transcript facilities now are working well. So we can proceed. The chunk that we missed before will be added later on in the day. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have LiveNote but I think I will continue to proceed with all deliberate speed so that everyone can follow along as I refer to both the English and the B/C/S versions. And again, we also need to leave a pause between our answers, that's as important as each of us speaking slowly. General, I want to turn your attention to a meeting you had -- actually a series of meetings, in April, specifically 20 April, where you met with both Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Serb officials, and why don't we just go directly to the report of that meeting. That's 65 ter 2936. Do you see the document, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Under the heading, "Meeting with Bosnian government officials," if we look at paragraph number 4, and that's on page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S, you and Mr. Akashi dealt with some demands of the Bosnian government, specifically that they had urged a more robust interpretation of the UNPROFOR mandate. And if you would just elaborate a bit upon what you and Mr. Akashi, what your response was to this urging to be more forceful in the execution of the mandate, and this proceeds from the bottom of page 4 to the top of -- I mean bottom of page 1 to the top of page 2 of both versions. If you could just explain for the Trial Chamber, perhaps in a little bit more detail, your response to the Bosnian Muslim officials and whether this was something that was an isolated demand on their part or whether this was something you had heard before from them.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. We had -- this wasn't isolated. This was a theme that you can trace back through much of the story of Bosnia, and UNPROFOR's involvement in it. Each of the parties would seek to use the UN and the UN forces in the country to their advantage. I had a phrase for this. I called it the hostage and shield situation. The -- in many respects, the Bosnians saw the UN as a very convenient source of their legitimisation, support for their population, and particularly with NATO a potential support for their cause in a military sense. The Bosnian Serbs saw the UN as a rather less of a shield and rather more of a hostage in more cases than not in that here was a means of controlling and influencing the international community, and I think this particular case is a manifestation of that in the particular set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we turn to paragraph 7, and this is page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, there is a summary, notes that attending this meeting were yourself, Mr. Akashi, President Karadzic, Messrs. Koljevic, Krajisnik and General Gvero. It indicates that the three major issues addressed were the extension of the cessation of hostilities agreements, the safety and resupply of UNPROFOR personnel and Sarajevo airport. Do you remember having a specific conversation with General Gvero during this meeting about the issue of fuel being restricted to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: If I recall it correctly, it was that fuel was being used, we were in effect supplying fuel to the defenders, to the Bosnians in the enclave, and that we had quite enough for our own purposes and that they, the Bosnian Serbs, were under -- were keeping a track of what we had and what we -- what was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say that the UN had enough fuel and reserves and so forth, who was making that statement, sir, just so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: That was General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could turn to paragraph 9? And that's on page 3 of both versions. That will be the next page of both versions. Under the heading of "Safety and Resupply of UN Personnel," it notes that Mr. Akashi raised the issues of direct attacks on UNPROFOR and the denial of supplies to UNPROFOR troops in the enclaves. Further on, the report notes that when questioned by General Smith on the matter of fuel General Gvero gave the rather inadequate explanation that he had intelligence that UNPROFOR and in particular UNPROFOR troops in Srebrenica were supplying the BiH with fuel. He further maintained that he knew that UNPROFOR had sufficient reserves and he persevered with this line in private discussions with General Smith after the meeting. General, does this passage accurately reflect what you recall occurring during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I mean that's broadly what I -- as I recall it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken a little bit about this already, but if we look at the top of that same page in the English, and we'll have to go back a page in the B/C/S to catch the bottom of the previous page in B/C/S, and I'll just read it again, there is a note that "We assess that he has still to make a formal decision to commit the Bosnian Serbs to war. However, the pressure on the Serb leadership and the cracks between the politicians and the military were very clear." Can you elaborate on that, General, from your recollection, with respect to cracks appearing between the Serb civilian and military leadership during there period of time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The -- my memory is at this stage is that we have a -- that we, that is I and my immediate staff, were forming the view, and this had been developing since February, that there was a degree of tension between the military and political within, in Pale, amongst the Bosnian Serbs. And exactly what this was about was never entirely clear to us, but we thought it was probably as to how much -- whether they should go on fighting or whether they should strike a deal now is essentially the point at issue, but I don't think we ever got enough information to suppose, to be firm in our own minds, as to which -- whether that was actually what the argument was about. The fact that I was having these meetings with Karadzic separately from and secretly were examples of why we thought that there might be a difference of view and so on within the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. And in this particular case, if I remember correctly, the -- it was over the actual airport itself, I think, and the opening of keeping it open and so forth that showed that the left hand wasn't entirely in communication with the right-hand, but the actual details of that I don't recall at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just look at one last portion of this report and see what your recollection is. If we look at paragraph 10, and that's on page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S so we need to -- that's it. Thank you. There is a reference to the Sarajevo airport, and it indicates that we noted that Krajisnik was clearly upset that the pledge he had made at a previous meeting the previous day to ensure that the necessary guarantees for UN civilians would be provided had not been honoured. This issue provoked some heated discussion between Karadzic and General Gvero. Do you have any recollection of this part of the meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Beyond the little I've alluded to, that I thought that that happened, I don't remember this particular case, particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to turn your attention just briefly to a meeting you had about 10 days later, on 30 April. This was again with Mr. Akashi, General Janvier accompanied you, and you were meeting with General Tolimir and President Karadzic and Messrs. Koljevic and Krajisnik. If we could have 65 ter 2937 on the screen, please, and I just want to call your attention to one portion on the third page of the document, paragraph 12, and we do not have a B/C/S translation of this document. I just want to call your attention to a couple of sentences, so I'll just read it into the record and hopefully you can see it when it comes up. And again, it's 2937. Oh, good. If we could look at paragraph 12, under "Other Issues," and again, that's page 6 of the translation, then. It refers to all three of you, Mr. Akashi, yourself, and General Janvier protesting the denial of fuel to the enclaves, to the eastern enclaves. Again, there is a reference to the Serbs persisting that UNPROFOR was providing supplies and fuel to the Muslims. And I want to ask you about this last sentence of note, Karadzic was heard to remark, "We regard humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys as commercial convoys for the benefit of the Muslims. We are under double restrictions, sanctions. You can expect more restrictions." What did you understand President Karadzic to mean by "double restrictions" or "sanctions" there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It is the -- you talk -- asked me a question earlier about UN sanctions. I believe this is what he's referring to, and the effects of not only Serbia being under sanction but the Bosnian Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn your attention to a meeting you had the next day. We are at 65 ter 2938. This is a meeting on May 1st attended by Mr. Akashi, yourself, President Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik. If we look at page 2 of the English and B/C/S, paragraph 7, if we can just scroll up on both versions, we will just note quickly who the participants were, Dr. Zametica was there as well, General Subotic. I want to direct your attention to the next page, that's page 3 of the English and also of the B/C/S. And we may need to take this a little bit more slowly than we've even been going already. We can scroll up a little bit. Under the heading, "Commander UNPROFOR Comment," just ask to you take a moment to read that portion to yourself and in particular the bottom paragraph that begins, "The Serbs are harder to read." Just take a moment. And this section will actually go on into the next page, so when you're ready for the next page just let us know, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Can we go over to page 4, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, I think for the most part this section speaks for itself pretty clearly, about your comments, your understanding of the situation at that time. Let me just call your attention to a couple of portions in particular, and while we are on this particular page, if we look at the second full paragraph, it states, "It is going to be important to recognise that the Serbs are reacting in part at least to this pressure and not to give into the counterpressure. We must be prepared for the long and painful haul if we intend to remain as peacekeepers." Towards the end of the paragraph, it says, "In light of what is anticipated will be difficult to manage so as not to lose the impartiality required of peacekeepers and avoid making matters worse. It may well be best when the opportunity occurs to play the 'air card' early in the game. "If it works, all well and good, if not, and with no evident willingness or immediate capability to escalate, UNPROFOR can close up and ride out the storm before matters become too dire." Would you elaborate a little bit for the Trial Chamber, please, what your thinking is there as you've expressed them in these comments?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: To set these remarks in context, the -- there is this whole series of meetings which are not mine, although it's my staff officer who is writing these records that we've seen. These are Mr. Akashi's meetings as he tries to establish or re-establish the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. I am there as a part of the meeting in support of Mr. Akashi. Nevertheless, I want all my subordinates to know what's happening, and as they are coming to an end, and this from memory is the last one, I want them all to know what I think as opposed to what -- and what this all might mean. And you must understand this is a running conversation, if you like. I've talked to them on the telephones, I've met them in between and so on and so forth. So this isn't -- these words are not standing on their own in the way that we are now looking at them. And they are also the view I had of that time, without of course, full knowledge of anything that was going to happen. So that's the sort of general background to it. You can see that the general -- my general understanding that I've talked of as the thesis is being confirmed, and I am already started to think and work out how we must behave in these circumstances and what we are to do, and really I'm recording there, particularly in that last paragraph, how I see things developing and what we, UNPROFOR, must be doing or thinking about doing into the future. More specifically, the -- we -- the general understanding of the role of UNPROFOR was as peacekeepers set within the idea of peacekeeping that had grown up during the Cold War, where essentially a military force with the agreement of both warring parties, is interposed to act as a barrier, if you like, between party A and party B. What we were doing with UNPROFOR in 1993, 1994, 1995, was to interpose a military force as peacekeepers under those -- under that previous understanding of the role and yet in the circumstances where the parties did not want to make peace, and yet we were being required to carry out certain functions, and increasingly during 1993, 1994, with the involvement of NATO, UNPROFOR had started to become more proactive in the use of force and a this was posing a number of political tensions within the capitals of the forces that -- of the countries that had provided forces to UNPROFOR and tensions within the Security Council and so forth; all of which I as a commander on the ground had to be understanding, had to understand. And that is why I am rehearsing this point about us being impartial, that the -- and that it may well be better to use the air card, in other words NATO, sooner rather than later so that if we haven't got the willingness to escalate in our capitals and to actually see this through, then we have done the least damage rather than to wait until the very last minute and discover that it doesn't work after all. And I think that was my thinking at the time and why those -- that paragraph is as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This in fact wasn't the -- not to be the last meeting. We do have notes from two others that I want to ask you some quick questions about. You had another meeting, a secret meeting with President Karadzic, on the 9th of May, and if we could just go directly to the report, it's 6D00163. And for this I will need the assistance of Madam Usher to put the B/C/S on the ELMO. This is a Defence Exhibit and the B/C/S hasn't, as I understand it, been loaded into e-court so we have a hard copy to place on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you have a translation of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, Ms. Stewart has been terribly helpful and cooperative, and she has organised these translations, we not having that obligation. But clearly when the Prosecution decides to use these documents, they as I say, organised the translations. For various reasons they haven't yet been put into e-court. We're in the process of doing that. They will have to go on the ELMO for the moment, but could I thank the Prosecution for their efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Josse, and thank you, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could just look at page 1 quickly, and that's a -- if we could scroll up just a little bit, I'm sorry, on the ELMO, I'm sorry, scroll down, that's good, thank you. Again, this is a meeting on 9 May, a secret meeting between yourself and President Karadzic. The paragraph 2 indicates that President Karadzic confirmed that the VRS had decided to put the UN under sanctions and that he gave the impression that opposed to a large counteroffensive, the VRS might be limited to a vigorous defence of their territory and comprehensive sanctions in the form of a blockade against the UN. Do you recall with any specificity what President Karadzic told you during this meeting about sanctions being imposed on the UN? And if you don't, we can just refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I do not with any -- no specific cases, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Usher, you need to put page 2, top of page 2, on the ELMO for the others to be able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 of the English, and I've given away my B/C/S so I'm not sure what page it's going to be of the B/C/S, but it's paragraph 5, if we can have that shown on the ELMO. There we go. As we can see here, President Karadzic again explained that he had been "convinced" by the VRS that the UN had ample fuel reserves in the enclaves. I think we just lost the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we just lost the ELMO. Okay. We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: President Karadzic had explained that he had been convinced in quotes by the VRS that the UN had ample fuel reserves in the enclaves, and as you've already testified that in Srebrenica, the Armija had built up a large supply of fuel from UN sources. The report indicates that you explained that you were certain that neither the Dutch nor the British contingents had supplied fuel to the BiH and that the situation was now so grave that the issue would soon "soon be out of your hands." General, what did you mean by that in this conversation that the matter or the issue would soon be out of your hands?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this is that the national -- the governments of the contingents in -- were beginning to become increasingly agitated and by the lack of supplies that the UN were beginning to -- were capable of managing for their forces, and I think I'm referring to that this would start to become a sort of a national matter, if you like, of the specific countries, and be taken away from the UN. But that's not a very strong memory but I think that's the background to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The last sentence of this paragraph reads, "When questioned about food, leave, and mail convoys, he," that's President Karadzic "confirmed that the Serbs had proposed their own 'resolutions' sanctions against the UN."
