Do you recall what problems, if any, there were with respect to I think you've already spoken about some of the food convoys, but how about the leave convoys?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, these were all in effects the same -- often the same trucks. It was what went on them. And when they would -- an empty truck on the way out would take a leave party out and soldiers would come back from leave on other vehicles and so forth. So I think this is more a question of what was being allowed or not allowed on vehicles rather than specific convoys as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 1 of the English, and I think that's going to be page 2 -- it's going to be paragraph 3, so if we can find the corresponding page on the B/C/S, under the heading, "NATO Air Strikes," towards the bottom of the paragraph in English, it indicates that Karadzic told you if NATO was used against the VRS, the BSA, he threatened that "Our relationship would disappear and we would treat you as the enemy." I think you've spoken about the development of your thesis up to this point. Was this statement to your recollection something different in any way or was this part of the same thing you were hearing up to that point?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It's to some extent it's more of the same. We were -- we, the UN, were to be pressured, denied access and so on and so forth. What -- what the difference in this particular case was that I read it or read it at the time as an attempt to divide me from NATO to split the UN and NATO from each other and not be seen as part and parcel of the same side. And he would say that, wouldn't he, because I was -- because the Bosnians were making it quite clear that they saw the advantage of the UN and NATO was NATO rather than the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2 of the English, and we'll need to scroll up just a little bit on the ELMO, please, Madam Usher, so we get that -- I'm sorry, scroll down so that we get that last line there, there is a comment that you make, if you just read that and is there anything you care to add or clarify with respect to this statement or this --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. I mean, it's -- I could see that we were being steadily drawn into a situation where we would be treated not just as an object to be sanctioned or pressured or squeezed in order to produce pressure. If we entered the game, we would -- in any forceful sense, were about to be put into the enemy paragraph of their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're at this point, if I could just ask you, the issue or the question might arise you've made reference to the idea of impartiality of UNPROFOR, and to your thinking at the time, what were the -- what were the factors that affected your ability to remain impartial? And can you discuss a little bit about this idea of impartiality? May as well do it now. I presume it's going to come up at some point so just take a moment, if you would.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The first point I'd make is that I don't understand impartiality and neutrality as being the same thing, although some do. The -- in the case of the situation at the beginning of 1995, and up until now, there were two -- there is the impartiality of the support of the delivery of humanitarian aid which was our initial and primary purpose. Here, I was not the -- I didn't choose who got the aid. That was the business of the UNHCR, and mine was to escort it, make sure it was safe or get it there. And I wasn't about to be drawn into an argument as to whether A should have that amount of food or B should have it. That was someone else's business, and I would see that it got there if I could. If I needed to use armed force to protect my forces while doing that, then I would use it, and I would use it insofar as it was necessary to defend my forces, and that act would stand alone. I certainly wouldn't be neutral when I was doing that. I would be attacking somebody. But I would -- it would not be being done for the purpose of altering the balance of forces in this particular conflict. It was being done to protect my command. With the inclusion earlier in the UNPROFOR Bosnia-Herzegovina story in -- of the no-fly zones, the exclusion zones around the safe areas and so forth, UNPROFOR, together with NATO, had been given the task of seeing that those strictures of the no-fly zone and the exclusion zone were maintained. And if they were broken, you could call upon military force to put the situation back to the status quo ante. The -- here again, you -- someone was going to have to, as it were, break the rules, break the safe area, break the exclusion zone, fly an airplane, before you could -- you would actually react to it militarily. So again, once you'd actually carried out -- were in that situation, you wouldn't be neutral, you would be attacking somebody, but your purpose wasn't to alter the balance between the two sides, it was to impose the exclusion zone and so forth. So that was essentially how one was trying to understand the situation that existed at the time. I can go on, but I think that's probably enough, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think so. Thank you, General. I want to ask you about one last meeting during this period of time, meeting which occurred on May 21st, again a secret, private meeting between yourself and President Karadzic. This is 6D00164. Again I'll need Madam Usher's assistance because we don't have the B/C/S translation loaded into e-court. General, if we could scroll down on the English to paragraph 3 and we'll have to adjust the B/C/S. Thank you, Madam Usher. And we'll skip the summary section and just go directly, and I think we'll have to actually go to the next page in B/C/S, that's the portion of the paragraph we'll be looking at. Thank you. Let me direct your attention specifically to the portion where you expressed your concern about the increasing targeting of UN personnel and the debilitating effect of the denial of supplies and movement to the eastern enclaves. And you pose the fundamental question to Karadzic as to whether the Bosnian Serbs wished the UN to remain in Bosnia. What was his response to that -- first that general question about remaining in Bosnia? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: There was two sides to it, as I recall it. One, that we, the UN, were very much part of the problem. We'd helped the enemy, the Bosnians, and we prevented the Bosnian Serbs from doing what they wanted to do. But on the other hand, they didn't want us to go in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just direct your attention to a couple of other areas and maybe expand on what you just said in light of those sections, if we could turn to page 2, and this is paragraph 4, so if we could find paragraph 4 in the B/C/S, thank you. Page 2 of the English. And this is specifically with respect to the eastern enclaves, General. At the bottom of the paragraph, President Karadzic referred to the enclaves as a "time bomb about to explode, and he maintained that the UN should get out of the eastern enclaves but also that UNHCR would be safe to remain." Do you recall him telling you that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Not -- I don't recall that particular exchange, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to page 3, to the comments section, this is page 3 of the English, and we'll have to adjust the ELMO to paragraph 10. The middle subparagraph at paragraph 10 states, these are your comments, "UNPROFOR remains the channel for the Bosnian Serbs to apply pressure on the international community, but they would like the UN out of the way in the eastern enclaves." Could you tell the Trial Chamber what you meant by this passage in the report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: This goes back to my understanding of the hostage and shield idea that I had mentioned earlier, that while the UN -- both sides sorry had a hostage and shield relationship with us, but of course they were different because of their different situations and purpose. But in this case, in the Bosnian Serbs, we were a source of as -- acting as a hostage, we could be squeezed, we could be used to influence the international community, the Security Council and so forth, to their advantage, but in order to be in that -- there and able to be influenced, we had to remain in reach of them. And so they needed us there at one hand as a shield, but as long as we were there as a shield, we could also be used as a hostage and both sides used us in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are done with this exhibit. Thank you, Madam Usher. General, you've already testified about your numerous protests about the increasing targeting of UNPROFOR and the attacks on civilian areas. Do you recall lodging any formal protests concerning this increased activity as opposed to stating them in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think these meetings were formal, but there were written protests on specific cases. I don't -- I know these were made. I made some of them. Others were made at sector level. It would -- depended on the circumstances and the severity of the particular case, but I don't recall specific ones, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at one, 65 ter 2939. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the -- actually of both, I guess, that will be helpful, great, okay. We can see that this is addressed from yourself to General Mladic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The date is 26 June 1995. I just direct your attention to the second paragraph where you state that "On an almost daily basis I am receiving reports of shelling of the populated areas of Bihac, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Sarajevo." And then skipping down a paragraph, "Apart from these attacks on the civil population, there is also an increasing number of reports of direct targeting of UNPROFOR locations and vehicles. Examples of these violations are recent attacks on observation posts in Gorazde, Srebrenica and Sarajevo." Do you recall, sir, the observation post being attacked in Srebrenica in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: If it's the answer I've already given you, the observation post that's overlooking that road I mentioned, then yes, I do, and that was attacked, as I remember it, by a tank or tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with that exhibit. Thank you. Now, sir, I want to talk briefly about some events that occurred in May, specifically the air strikes of 25 and 26 May, the last meeting notes that we looked at were dated May 21st, and I just showed you something from June 26th. So some fairly significant events occurred in that month or so. So I want to talk just a little bit about the air strikes of May 25th and May 26th and the hostage-taking by the VRS of UNPROFOR personnel afterwards. I don't want to get into a dissection of those events at all but I want to ask you, I think because it's more relevant for our purposes here, could you describe how the air strikes and their aftermath, the hostage-taking, affected your thinking, your thesis, and how air power was to be employed after those events. I think you alluded to it a little earlier in your testimony, but if you could pick that up just for a little while so that we could talk about that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: During May, a series -- there were a series of incidents and as the situation deteriorated further and further. And by the end of May, the Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo were using weapons that had been taken from or were being used from weapon collection points, and using them to attack targets within the safe area of Sarajevo. There had been a series of warnings, of protests and so forth. And I came to the conclusion that -- during this month and you've seen the beginnings of it starting to form in my mind, that it now is the time that we had to enforce this exclusion zone and if we didn't get on with it we weren't going to have that option open to us any more. There was considerable pressure on -- to do this because the fighting had increased and so on. I -- you had to do this in consultation with NATO, all of that took place, you had to get the authorities from Mr. Akashi above, and that was all done, and the idea was to use air power, not to attack the specific weapons, which were extremely difficult to attack, locate, but to influence the decision makers in Pale into stopping to do this, stopping to use the weapons in the exclusion zones and break the exclusion zone resolution, but also attacking the populated areas of Sarajevo. These attacks, there was a warning given,, the attacks were -- took place; and that night, after the attacks, there was a response to these attacks by the Bosnian Serbs with artillery being fired into all of the safe areas. I may have got that wrong. It may not have gone into Bihac, but I think it went even into there. The most destructive of those attacks killed some 70 people in Tuzla. In my planning, I had planned that if we didn't succeed in the first go, we would escalate, and this had been approved. We did a second series of air attacks, which led to a number of hostages being taken almost at once, television pictures of them being chained to I think a radio mast and a bridge, and an immediate world wide international reaction. I was told to stop doing what I was doing, and that was it. The -- over the next 24 hours, some 300 hostages, I can't remember the exact number, were taken. You then enter a period, which runs all the way up to the middle of July, when UNPROFOR is recalibrating, is one way of describing it, I suppose, of -- as to just what it is we can do and so are the UN commanders and political -- the SRSG and so forth, above me, establishing what it is UNPROFOR is to be doing at that period, immediately after May. Is that enough of a general outline for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General. I want to bring us forward now to July of 1995. I don't think there is any dispute that the VRS attack on the enclave began on or about the 6th of July. Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I'm on leave in Korcula.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long you'd been on leave by 6 July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I think I'd been on leave a little under a week. I can do it by days. I went on leave over a weekend and I don't know what day the 6th of July was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. When you were on leave, General, did you stay in contact with your command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I had a radio link with me, and an operator and a bodyguard that went with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall, approximately, how often you stayed in touch with your command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Initially, as I remember, it was every day, I'd take a call. But as things hotted up, and after the middle weekend of the two weeks' leave I had, I was in much more frequent contact, and I was recalled from leave to go to Geneva over that -- the middle weekend of my leave and to meet with the Secretary-General. So I was briefed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll talk a little bit briefly about Geneva. But during this period of time when things were beginning to heat up, with whom were you actually in contact from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I was in contact with my military assistant, Colonel Baxter. My -- General Bobar the sector Sarajevo commander had assumed command in my absence, but I left the military assistants there so that there was couldn't knew wit my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has already heard a bit of testimony about the JCOs who were deployed throughout Bosnia and in the Srebrenica enclave as well. Would you please talk a little bit about this JCO programme, when it began, what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: JCO is joint commission observers, if I recall correctly, is their title. They -- when General Rose had been the commander, he had established this group of people, acting largely in Sarajevo, and as a link with the Bosnian Serbs. They had been included, if I recall correctly, in the -- in the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement at the end of 1994, as part of the observer and control mechanisms, if you like, of that -- of that agreement. They were -- their value to me, as the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement broke down, was much more to do with their communications and their ability as forward air controllers. And as it got harder and harder to communicate with the enclaves, the more important it was that I had a reliable form of communication with those enclaves, and so I deployed JCO teams into Srebrenica and Gorazde. I don't think we got one into Zepa at all, but I can't remember that. The reason of them -- the points about them being forward air controllers is that the NATO nations had forward air controllers in their units who were practised and certified to operate with NATO air forces. This was not the case with some of our troop contributing nations who didn't have -- who didn't come from NATO. So that was one reason for wanting them there. Secondly, to keep this certification, you have to be at a degree of practice with so many missions, practised and so forth. And one of the consequences of the restrictions on movement was that the units in the enclaves were losing their currency to handle NATO airplanes, and so this, too, became reason for getting the JCOs into the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, with respect to the JCOs who were in the Srebrenica enclave, do you recall whether they were there secretly or whether they had been declared to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I am -- they certainly weren't there secretly in that we couldn't have got them in there without them driving there, and I have no -- I don't recall how we told -- said who they were and so forth, but they were quite clearly not Dutch. They must have got in somehow, and they must have been seen going in. And the -- they tended to use a particular point of contact in -- I can't remember his rank, but he was called Indic in Lukavica. I suspect that we told him and that's how they went in. And if they had been that secret, I suspect there would have been a lot more fuss after Srebrenica had fallen, but there wasn't and they just came out with the Dutch unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall during these events of the attack on the enclave whether you received any information that you can recall directly tied to these JCOs who were operating in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Not -- if you mean that I communicated with them directly, no. I don't think I ever did. And I don't remember a specific report that, you know, someone carried to me with this has come from that team. I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to your recall from leave to go to Geneva. Was that recall tied directly to the Srebrenica attack or was it for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. It was wholly for some other reason. It was the report to the Security Council, it was to discuss the report to the Security Council, and the recommendations as to what UNPROFOR should be doing. The Zagreb draft for this had been sent off sometime in late May, to which we in Sarajevo had contributed, and this meeting was to finalise that report for the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you return to your leave after that or did you go back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. We -- I went back on leave. We had -- during this meeting with Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali, I can't remember the precise details but I think it was the loss of another OP and a Dutch soldier being killed was reported to us, was told to us. And the -- the general understanding of what was happening in Srebrenica was that this was a fight about the road I mentioned and it was an example of further squeezing of the enclave rather than what it turned out to be, it was a misappreciation of what was happening. And I recall asking whether both General Janvier and Mr. Akashi whether they wanted me to return from leave and go to Sarajevo, and I was told, no, stay on leave and finish your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I flew back or down to Split and from there out to Korcula, and then I think it's a day later I am recalled from leave and start a 24 to 36 hour journey of getting back into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did you return, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Because the -- as I say, the situation had been misappreciated. This attack developed much more strongly. The defence collapsed. The -- and the enclave fell as a defensive position and we had a whole load of refugees and so forth all around the Dutch Battalion in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I want to show you a report of a meeting. Do you recall meeting with Minister Silajdzic on the 13th of July during the course of your return from leave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I do remember. I was -- I'd been back for a bit of time by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let me call up the document. It's 65 ter 2941.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I find that very difficult to read. If you've got the hard copy there?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could scroll up on the B/C/S as well, please. I want to direct your attention to paragraph 3 first, Silajdzic immediately raised the issue of Zepa and asks you whether you could reinforce the UN forces there. And you replied that you had neither the capability nor the orders to do so at that time and you emphasised that currently your most important task was to clarify the policy on the enclaves and identify the stance of the participating member states as whatever action was taken in Srebrenica would become the model for the other enclaves. Can you expand on those two sections a little bit, General, please? What did you mean when you said you had neither the capability nor the orders to reinforce?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the latter is easily explained. I had no orders to reinforce any of the enclaves, let alone Zepa. And I certainly didn't have any spare forces, always assuming that the contributing nation was prepared for me to put them into Zepa. That's the, you know, first-order essence or answer to what I'm saying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 5 of the English and that's on page 2 of the B/C/S, you have a discussion with the minister about the use of the Tuzla air base for the refugees arriving from the enclave. And you explain that you had sent your deputy Chief of Staff, Colonel Coiffet to aid in effort to coordinate the resources. Do you recall dispatching Colonel Coiffet to do that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have any reservations about the air base being used?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't -- if -- would it help if I gave a bit of the background? We've had this catastrophe. We've -- a complete enclave has collapsed. There is a large number of refugees to be handled, and a number that we're not entirely clear as to how many are involved. And all the military and deterrent effects such as they were of UNPROFOR and for that matter NATO, have been neutralised by these events. So as I say in an earlier part of my -- I think I'm saying it there, trying to understand what the policy is on -- and so forth. I imagine it's to clarify the policy on the enclaves and identify what the member states are actually capable or willing to do because it was quite clear that they are not -- they are not doing what they said they were going to do. The -- at the same time, the Bosnians are using this as an opportunity to beat up the UN and are refusing to help with any of these hostages -- sorry, refugees, that have been starting to flood over the front line between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnians. And I am -- I've got to put them somewhere. And the only large empty space I've got is Tuzla or the airfield with some military there capable of building, putting up tented camps and so forth but it's not the best place for a refugee -- masses of refugees to go. It just happens to be the only space I've got at that time. And much of my subsequent effort is trying to get the Bosnians to start to take responsibility for all of these people or share the responsibility of all these people and stop using something -- somewhere between 25 and 30.000 refugees as something as a stick to beat the UN with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 6 on page 2 of the English, and that's also on page 2 of the B/C/S, refers to, "Both the Prime Minister and Minister Muratovic raised their concerns as to the as-yet-unconfirmed reports of atrocities in the Srebrenica area, in particular the rape of young women in Vlasenica and the murder of a busload of refugees." There is another reference further down, "They are also worried about reports of refugees being segregated into groups and men between the ages of 60 and 16 being sent to different locations." Now, I know, General, that this meeting occurred at 1420 hours on 13 July. Do you recall when you first heard reports of atrocities in the aftermath of the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I don't, in -- I don't have a specific memory. I'm -- this is the -- this would be amongst the first and probably the first from a Bosnian source, in that I've only got in in the early hours of this morning into -- into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we scroll down on the English to paragraph 9, and we'll have to skip to the next page of the B/C/S to pick up that paragraph. There is a reference in the first line, paragraph 9, that you raised the issue of the move of elements of the MNB upcountry from Tomislavgrad to the Kresevo-Tarcin area. Can you just elaborate on what is happening there and what -- first of all, what's the MNB?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The MNB is a multi-national brigade, and this is a -- part of and it's headquarters commanded the rapid reaction force. This force has its origins in the events immediately after the bombing in May, 25, 26, when I formed two units, one British, one French, from the forces in theatre, in, as they were armoured infantry battalions and they had tasks to be ready to react and move and operate in each other's areas and gave me a small force under my own hand. The British had reinforced this unilaterally, almost immediately I had started to form these forces, and somewhere around the middle of June, the Security Council have -- had a resolution mandating a rapid reaction force for the better protection of UNPROFOR, if I remember its terminology correctly. The French also produced some extra forces and these are starting to -- these start to be deployed during June, and here is some of them appearing in the south of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the difference between the rapid reaction force and the MNB?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the rapid reaction force was more than just the multi-national brigade. There was an artillery group, there was a portable brigade as well. And they -- they were -- they were held, as it were, separately from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this period of time in which the Srebrenica enclave fell, how operational was the full rapid reaction force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: It was not yet fully deployed or operational at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And had you encountered any opposition or suspicion from either of the warring parties about the rapid reaction force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: The Federation was suspicious of it because they thought it could be used against them. And I think largely at this stage the Bosnian Serbs were less worried about it because I think they thought they could control UNPROFOR by taking hostages and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, what was your view of this rapid reaction force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: If I was to use this force, I had to -- it had to be understood by those I wished to use it against as not being under my hand. Otherwise, they could neutralise it by taking hostages and so forth. So it was very important that this was a force that was understood to be separate from UNPROFOR and part of another command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this reference in this document to the MNB moving up country, was that in relation at all to the developments in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: No. This was us getting it into the theatre and establishing it. It had yet to form as a -- as its -- and deploy fully into the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So how would you describe your ability during the period in which the Srebrenica enclave was attacked to make use of the MNB or the RRF?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH
utterances.text: I couldn't have used them in that -- in those circumstances, if I'd been there. And secondly, the -- even if they had been, I'd -- we wouldn't have been able to reach Srebrenica with the forces that were available in the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are nearing the break. I think this would be a good place to stop. I'm about to move into a different area, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are nearing the end of the sitting. Now, what's the position? When will the general be back?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will be ready to roll tomorrow, Mr. President and for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So we are going to have him the rest of the week? Okay. All right. That's fine. Tomorrow, General, we'll be sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow afternoon at 2.00 [sic]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
